titleStmt.author: David Emory and Cynthia S. Hyatt [transcriber]

bibl.title: Interview with Ronald R. Pittenger
bibl.author: David Emory and Cynthia S. Hyatt [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Ronald R. Pittenger was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Apparently there is a few things I've got to start with, some formalities. Okay.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And it says here I've got to obviously introduce myself. My name is David Emory, and today is March 31st, 2012. And I'm conducting an oral history interview with Ronald --let me get the full name.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Ronald Ray Pittenger, is that right?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And the court reporter today is Cindy. And your last name?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Hyatt. Okay. Sir, at this time can you tell me what your date of birth is?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Second of June, 1924. Okay. And the branch of your service? That will be Army, I think, right?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And the date of your service?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, I went in on the 9th of September, I believe it was.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And what date did I retire?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And he got retired in August '69.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And that's what he looked like.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: There you go. All right. Now, again, I'm going to ask you some questions that seem a bit repetitive. Can you please state your name and the address where you are living?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And we're here at Air Force Village I, is that right?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: The street address, if you need it for the record, is 4917 Ravenswood Drive, and our apartment is 1110.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Great. Where were you born?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: They say it is not even there is anymore.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Wow. Gee willikers. Okay. And what is the name of your parents?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And my --you want my mother's maiden name?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Gustafson, huh. Okay. And do you have any brothers or sisters?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I have got a brother and a sister.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Brother is the same birth date as mine and a year later, and my sister is a year and a week later.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Then his mother got the word.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Did you grow up in Goff?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No, I grew up in Sabetha, Kansas.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Got it. Okay. Were your parents in the military?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Was he in the Army?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: In World War I and World War II.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He was Air Corp in World War II.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He was Air Corp in World War II.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Uh-huh. And were any of your brothers and sisters in the military?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Put your hands down, sweetie. It makes it easier.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And he never was commissioned or anything. He --when the war ended, they asked him if he wanted to stay in the Navy and fly, and he said, No, and he got out, and that was it.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I couldn't. I went in at a time when you couldn't enlist. You had to go through the draft board.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I didn't know that. Good questions.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Yeah. I'll be darn. And were you living in Kansas at the time?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: May I throw one in? His sister was married to someone that was military, also. Tom Reed. You know, Cindy and I were talking about if this is --you know, if anybody can draw up their family name, that would be a cross reference thing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: So Tom was in the Marines, Tom Reed.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: In the Marines --in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, and served in the South Pacific.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Can you tell us why --well, I guess you were drafted so you didn't have much of a choice, but can you tell me why you joined the Army?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --but it was at a time when --when you had to go through the draft board. You couldn't --you just couldn't go down and enlist. You had to go through the draft board to volunteer, which I did.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Just thing to do, that's all. The war was going on. It was hot and heavy.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Why did you --why did you pick the Army over any other services?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Because my father was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: World War II. He was in World War I, and then World War II he was in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: It wasn't the Air Force until after.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, he was in China with the -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Do you recall the first days when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Can you tell me a little bit about that? What was that like?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, I will never forget that. Fort Leavenworth, there were just barracks were just thrown up.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No insulation or anything. Two potbellied stoves in each barracks. Somebody had to stay awake all night feeding it.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And I was glad to leave there.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Wow. Tell me, your boot camp and boot camp training, where was that? Was that also in Kansas?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No, I --from there I went to Camp Wallace, Texas, which is down close to -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about the experiences in boot camp.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Put your hands down, sweetie. She can't hear you.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It wasn't strange to me because I had been around the Army with my dad, who was in the National Guard, and I would go to camp every year with him, and I would shine their shoes and all of that stuff. And so I was pretty familiar with it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He was --we were trying to figure last night. He was 12 or 13, and his dad was in the horse calvary, and so -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Horse artillery. Didn't you do a few more things around the horses besides just polish the boots with the guys? Didn't you do a little poop scooping?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I cleaned up after the horses.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Golly. Do you remember any of your instructors at boot camp?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I remember them, but I don't remember the names.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Can you tell --tell me where you were awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, I came out with two Silver Stars, three Bronze Stars, Unit Citation.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I have got his whole list of medals there.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: The list I'm going to show you is a list of all your citations and medals, is that right?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: So you were in the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Yep. That was some tough times.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Turning point of World War II.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Right, no question. Where did you get your Silver Stars?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: One of them over the Saar River when we were crossing there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I said the Saar is spelled S-A-A-R.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And I would have to look and see where the other one was.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Absolutely. Follower of world history, one of which was World War II, so that's pretty amazing.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Here is --let me see. This is a Bronze Star. I can pull the others. We just didn't know how much to give you. This one is Korea. It is not the Silver Star. He got the --he got the award because he was a combat engineer with the 55th Armored -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: --group attached to the 10th Armored Division under General Patton. One of them he got for affecting a --building the bridge to cross. The Germans had blown it up, and so the engineers had to go in so that the service troops and the tanks could get across the bridge. So he helped --well, he led his platoon, and they built the bridge. And it got blown up, and they built it again. And it got blow up again. But eventually they helped long enough that they could get the troops across was one of them. Another one was the opposite. Another Silver Star is when --I think I have it here --the bridge had been I guess you would call it booby-trapped, Ron, by the Germans.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And the troops could not go across because they had left five bombs hanging under the bridge. And so he and his sergeant hand-walked out and released the bombs into the water so that the troops could go across. And, of course, he was lucky they didn't --he says --in his memoirs he says, I guess they're still there because they didn't blow up.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Golly. Now, you have prepared a memoir or an outline of his affairs?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: I would like to have that included, too.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, that's the thing I'm questioning. There is two things. One of them I marked in pink here.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And it is sort of in that area, so and I'm going to read it to you so we know what we are talking about, but not for publication.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Right. [Off the record discussion] [End of Audio File 1] [Beginning of Audio File 2]

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Back on the record. We have been speaking about your experience in the war, and it is understood, obviously, since this has got to be a record, that this is --right now we are speaking about your life in World War II, is that right?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. If you can remember some of the instances of your experiences in World War II, if you could tell me one memorable battle or incident or operation that might come to mind I would appreciate it.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, I probably could. I think when we crossed the Saar River, and it was in the what they call the Saar-Moselle Triangle.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: The Saar River goes one way and Moselle goes the other, and I mean they sort of go like that. And all --all the rivers in Europe flowed north. They flow north. See, here in the states they flow south. And so all of our rivers were --they were cold. And I made a lot of crossings of them, building bridges, swimming the river sometimes to take over --to build from that side, just things like that.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Who --what unit were you attached to?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about who was involved in that 10th Armored for the record. Who is our commanders there?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: His name was Morris. I can't say the name.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Maybe you're part of Patton's units?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. And he was --general was a classmate of Eisenhower's.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And so he got --just to get on his record was a problem. I don't know what it was. He was the poorest general I ever met.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And you were in the engineer division?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: We, if they came to an obstacle, the tanks -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --we would go up and take it apart so they could get through -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --the tanks. And sometimes it was just --the Germans made a log. They cut these big trees, and then they built this thing around them where they just pile them up, and you couldn't get through them.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: So they put it in a gully where you couldn't go around. If you did, you had to go quite a ways around. And it was just --just slowed us down. That's all.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Uh-huh. And your battalion then was in charge of doing what, removing those obstacles?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: My assignment was part of the 55th --it was the 55th Armored Engineer Battalion.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Tell me a little bit about Bastogne. Tell me how that whole --how you got involved in that --in that battle.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, we were on the outskirts of -we were in Bastogne, and we knew the Germans were all around us.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And we were trying to get out of Bastogne, our little company, the engineer company. And we kept trying to get out, and they had us surrounded, of course.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And we couldn't get out. We finally found a village. There were no Germans in it, and so we hold up there until they cleared off and they could bomb again and get in there. That's about all it was.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What was the experience like? Tell me a little bit. For a person who has never experienced battle, what was it like in Bastogne while you were there?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It was cold and we didn't have winter gear.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: They --it hadn't come up yet, and it was so --and it was just miserable. That's all.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: We fought them off if they came after us. We tried to get out of Bastogne, my company did, and we couldn't get out.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: We would go a couple of miles and turn a corner and here would be a tiger tank. They would shoot off about two rounds, go right over our head, and we would turn around and go back, try to go out that a way. Finally we just couldn't do it, just couldn't get out. And they had us --completely surrounded us.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What other battles were you in besides the Battle of the Bulge?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, I was in combat from then on, and we split off and went south to Garmisch.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --were held there just before the war, I think, because the ski --ski towers and everything were still there, and we --we had a dwarf, Obsey, and we got up there in a big hotel, and we took over the hotel, and they made it a rest camp. And the Zugspitze is right there. Have you heard of the Zugspitze? It is the largest, highest mountain in Germany. And they had a trolley that would take people up to the top of it. You could see --I forget how many countries you could see. But later on I'm back to the war in World War II. After there I was in Germany, and I hunt a lot. And I used to hunt there. And we would go up to Zugspitze looking for different deer and different animals to hunt and --lost my track here. But anyway -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What other --after you went to Bastogne, where did you go?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I had my --my feet were frozen, and I became infected. And I was on the way to Europe, to South Pacific after the war. It was still going on in the South Pacific. And my feet just got swollen. I couldn't walk or do anything and went to the hospital. And I never went to South Pacific. I was in the hospital in Paris.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: In Paris. And when the war was over, I was assigned to the --it was the unit --we discharged people. One would be discharged overseas in Paris, and we discharge them there. And we discharged about, oh, 15 to 30 a day that wanted to stay in France. And then I left there. I came on home.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: How did you get into Europe when the war --when we invaded Europe, did you go through Normandy?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Were you one of the original -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Not the --well, I said north. Yes, I did. It was --trying to remember now.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: I guess you guys were originally stationed in England, right?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No, I never was in England.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I have never been in England.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I have been to Germany three times.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Did you say that you landed in Cherbourg three months after Normandy?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: That's what we were just getting to.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Tell me about that. Did you -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: There is nothing to it. They were already --had a beach there and everything. I mean, it was --we got a few bombings at night, you know.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And that's all. Just be a lone --be a lone German ship --plane would fly over and drop a couple of bombs, and we would sit there and hope they didn't hit you.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And then from there you went through to Bastogne?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Was it before that the --the --if you don't know what it was, actually, but if the -the bomb that was the noise thing that the Germans had.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: We would call them the Screaming Mimi --Mimi.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It was --it was a border shell that made the damndest noise you ever heard.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And you just --when you heard it, you got under cover somewhere.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: But you also had another thing that I had forgotten about that I was reading the other night about the German plane that, you know, played cat and mouse with you. You were out in the field and this German plane just kept you -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Ran me all over the field.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: It is like that movie, you know, where the guy is out in the field. It was just exactly.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, I would just go from one --one corner to the next, and German plane would come around, and I was all on the jeep, the driver. So we got in the corner of a field and was ditch all the way around it. So he would come at us. We would get in ditch where he couldn't hit us. And then he would come back. We would get in the other ditch until we finally --I was running out of gas, I guess. He flew off.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What rank were you during this time?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And, once again, once you left Bastogne and you went to the hospital because of your feet, right?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Were you stationed any other place after Bastogne or after you got your feet well?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: In Paris. Okay. That had already been occupied by us?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, yeah, and I was a deputy --I don't know what you would call it. Separation center. We discharged people over there.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And we would take --do all the paperwork and everything for them. I had clerks and people that take care of me sort of thing.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: After you went to Paris, were there any other front line assignments that you had?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He has --I jogged your memory about something that I thought was interesting, and that was when you were at Bertesgarten and you did a little recon in the jeep and found the hotel with the blonde women.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you go to the Bertesgarten?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And I was out one day with my driver, and we --we were going up this mountain road. I was just looking at things because from where we were we could see Italy -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --and --and the other countries down there. And then we got to a place, and it had been --the bridge had been blown out. We tore two big planks there, so we put them across and drove the jeep over it and went on up. And here was this hotel with some of the most beautiful women you have ever seen, blonde hair. And -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He always tells the blonde part.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It was really, really something else. And we discovered it was a rest camp for German officers, and all of these women were up there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Some pregnant, some not, but it was to perpetuate the German -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Etiology or something, or something, yeah.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, and biology, too, blue-eyed blondes.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you --your wife was saying that you had gone to the Bertesgarten after the war?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. That would have been in Hitler's --one of Hitler's retreats or -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Right? What was that like? Tell me a little bit about what you observed.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, it was the --the hotel he went to was on the --I forget the name of the mountain, but it was one of the tallest mountains down there. It wasn't Bertesgarten, but that was one of them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: It was this --Gosh, what was the name of his retreat? Eagles Nest.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: This was right after the war?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Now, were you --did you stay in Germany or in Europe right after the war as an occupying force? THE WITNESS: Yeah, until -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And we had to have so many points to get home, and I was just on the edge of not having enough points to go home.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: So I had to stay there, and I went to Paris, and I was --we had a separation center there with the Army in Paris, and stayed there while I came home.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you have occasion as to --seems like an obvious question --to involve yourself in observing large casualties during the war when you were in front line?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about that?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: You don't want to talk about that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You know, he says that, and he was. Nowadays he would have been wounded.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He was under a tank when they fired --what did they fire?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You know, the --what did they fire?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What was --tell me a little bit about that story. What happened?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, we got --it was in the Saar-Moselle Triangle, and we were trying to get across the Moselle River, and we had been across the Saar already. And I crawled out underneath the tank that was on the edge of this bridge that had been blown to see how wide the bridge was and what --how much bridging I need to get across it. And just as I got under the --I told the tank driver, I said, Don't do anything now. I'm going to be under the -so they have a place --I don't know which -MRS. PITTENGER: Affect.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Affect. And it --all firing stuff comes down and the shell goes out. And I told this tanker, I said, I'm going out there on the edge of this bridge and don't you shoot until I come back. Well, I got out there and he shot.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: So it all went down on him.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It was -MRS. PITTENGER: So he had a concussion, but he kept going.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah. I couldn't hear anything for a couple of days.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You know, there is very definitely some VA studies now of the correlation -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: --between concussions and other head memory problems later on.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: But, and you left out the parts that I like. He got his pants shot off of him three out of seven nights because they kept him going on the amphetamines and the --you know. And the other part that just --this is an aside, but I don't care if it is recorded or not. You know, they kept giving him cigarettes. You know, they come back, give him cigarettes, give him something to drink, da-da-da, and so forth. Now any time that you put in these old timers, when they put in for a benefit, they say, Well, a lot of your problems were because you smoked so much. Okay. Give me a break. They knew --I mean, nobody expected them to live anyway, and they're giving them those cute little packages of cigarettes. And we just got another thing back that his heart thing was probably, you know, as a result of his smoking. Well, let's see. Were you under stress?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Let me think. I don't think so.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: You were never a prisoner of war, correct? THE WITNESS: No.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Did you happen to take any prisoners yourself?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about that.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, there's not much to it. When we take, the armored division, you go fast. You take prisoners. You turn them to the guy behind you, and you take off. You didn't know what happens to them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You didn't know what happened to them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Because he was in the front line, and they passed them back to them.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. So you were directly attached to a tank battalion as an engineer unit?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Building bridges or removing obstacles for the forward tank units -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Anything to stop the tanks, we had -we went up to see what we could do to get around them. We would try to go around them, whatever. Just depended because the thing about it then they would put a log across the highway.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, they put a log usually in place, or they would find a place where there was a bridge, blow the bridge so they couldn't get across, anything to stop the tanks from going across. And as an engineer platoon leader, it was my job to get them --when they got stopped like that was to get them past it some way. I mean, sometimes I build a bridge. Sometimes I just find a way around.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Your tanks were primarily a Sherman tank, as I recall?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What type of tanks did you guys -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Yeah. What did your tankers think about the German armor?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did they ever tell you anything, any stories about those German tanks?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, actually, I saw a few of them.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What do you think about them?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I don't think they were near as good as ours. They were just bigger, that's all. They had one that had a 150-millimeter cannon on it. And I was making a recognizance, and during that Christmas break when the Germans had the cannons out, and I went around a corner and ran into three German Tiger tanks.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Uh-huh. And I immediately --they immediately shot at me, but everything was over my head. And my driver --I turned around and we took off from there fast as I could, but they had good tanks.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Now, I heard in the earlier on in our first introduction that you had made reference about Korea. Were you subsequently in Korea?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Tell me a little bit about your -your experiences in Korea.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, I was --when I got over there, I was a company commander of an infantry company. We were all on a line. Then the war was a stagnant war. Everything was stopped. And I was there for about -how long? Did I say in there how long I was there?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I guess about a month, and I got a call from the regimental headquarters, and they wanted to see me. And I went back and they had made me assistant to the chief of staff of the division -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --because the guy that came in --I was the captain at the time, and this guy was a major. And my regimental commander was --was a former CO of this major and wasn't good with his outfits, so they traded me for him. And I got to be --I was the assistant to the chief of staff in the 40th Division in Korea.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, Ron, did you talk about being a company commander on --in Korea in the Punch Bowl next to Luke's Castle -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: --or any of the above? It is in the notes that I gave y'all on Korea.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It was a big bowl, mountains all the way around it. You come over the bridge line any direction, and there was this big bowl, and so it was --it was called a Punch Bowl in Korea.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: And that's about all I can tell you about it. It was a lot of battles fought there in Korea.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Were you front line officer, as well?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And you had 350 Republic of Korea troops under you, as well as yours?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah. No, I didn't. You tell them.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I was just reading what you wrote.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you have some Republic of Korea troops under you?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What were they like? What was it like to have kind of a dual leadership?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I never had any anything at all. All they did was fill sand bags, build stuff that I wanted built. I didn't have anything to do with them. They were --they had their own officers.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: They had their own discipline, too.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: For example, I came down the hill one day and went down by where they were. They were camped, and here was three soldiers spread out on the ground.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Koreans. And legs and hands were side out like this, and they were being whipped, and nothing I could do. We would never do nothing like that.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What was their infraction? What did they do wrong?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I thought you told me they stole some things. THE WITNESS: Oh, they stole something from somebody, but I don't know what it was. They stole something from one of our groups, I guess.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: How long were you in Korea?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yeah, we were married at the time.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: There was --there is a picture --I thought I had them with this grouping. Ron and one of the other guys went back to Japan, and they made a punch bowl that is now in possession of the 40th Armored National Guard, and the punch bowl duplicates the terrain in silver of the Punch Bowl, the actual geographical Punch Bowl.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Yes, from the 40th Division. The 40th Division was National Guard from California.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Here it is. There is the punch bowl.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Why were you assigned to the 40th Division California National Guard?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, I was overseas. They were already overseas, and I was, too. And that's --they were just a unit I was assigned to.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Because they were active duty, same as anybody. It wasn't -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. After the war, did you go back to school or -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Did you use your GI bill?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I used the GI bill. I didn't like it so I quit.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Went into the lumber business down in Missouri.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I'm sorry. I was reading your -oh, Korea broke out and you volunteered to go in after we had been married seven months.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: So after World War II, you -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: You went to college, did you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Engineering school, and then he went into the lumbar business in Southern Missouri, and then he came to the town that I lived in, and then you were active duty for the Missouri National Guard because -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: --it was to compare it to nowadays, he took all the troops in that area that had been deployed and reassembled them so that they were once again home, you know, National Guard as opposed to active duty troops.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And so they --you know, and he was full-time. He was in uniform. That's what got me. And prepared him to go to summer camp and do that sort of thing, and then Korea broke out, and he volunteered to go back on active duty.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Why would you volunteer to go back on active duty after World War II?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Yeah, but you had already gone and fought in a big war.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I know, but I couldn't tell you why then.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I just like the life. That's all.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Do you know what he said? He said, I know how to fight, and I know how to save lives, and I have had the experience, and I know if I go there that I can help save some lives.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You know, it really sounds funny, but these guys are flag wavers.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I get a little jaundiced, but they don't.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you --we will focus on World War II for just one more second, and then we will go into Korea again. They're asking me, did you, you know, make any close relationships while in the service in World War II, any best buddies or best buds or close acquaintances?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, I had some, but we didn't --we never followed up.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: I never saw any of those guys later.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Anybody you remember in World War II that you were close with during the war?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, my company commander's name. Guy by the name of Garwood, and he was from Colorado, an engineer. And then I had -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And he was killed coming up to see Ron.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He was killed in battle coming up to see you, Garwood. Isn't he the one that was killed?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No, I can't remember who it was now. So long ago.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And you didn't keep touch with any of the colleagues in World War II?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Not really. I heard from this Garwood for a couple of Christmases, but that was it.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: What about in Korea? Were there any friendships or close colleagues that you got to know?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: That idiot that used to park his car on our front porch.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Uncle Herb, as our son would call him, Herb Mansfield. Colonel Herb Mansfield.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: G3 of the 40th Division and became a close friend of mine because I did bunch of stuff with him. And I was a captain and he was lieutenant colonel at the time and was a life-long friend. Used to come by and visit us and helped our son. Used to pick him up and put two of those pillows, one under him and one on top of him, and say I'm going to have a bun.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: But he was just a real good friend.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Did you join any veterans' organizations?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: He feels very strongly about supporting the DAV, though, because they do a lot of good for people.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: But he is not the go-down-to-the-legion-I'll-drink kind of guy.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Now, how did your service and experience affect your life after the war?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You're sort of at the point now that when he came --after Korea and he came back. Then, of course, he went to another military school, levels of schools that you go on up, but then because he had had so much combat experience, personnel tapped him. And so first they sent him to parachute jump school where he had a compound fracture of his back but didn't acknowledge it because he wanted to be able to graduate. And then he went to flight school, Army Aviation Flight School.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And he was also picked because of his command experience to command the 82nd Airborne Aviation Unit that was doing experimental training. Am I right?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And it was called the Howze, or General Howze, H-O-W-Z-E, picked him to do this. So when you asked Ron what branch he was before, it is kind of funny because he has been armor, engineer, infantry, aviation, and paratrooper, you know, all of the above. When he gets dressed up, you should see it.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: But that was --that was another whole --it was like it wasn't another war. And then when Vietnam came, they wouldn't let him go because he had so much command experience, and his contemporaries that were the West Pointers had, through no fault of their own, had just missed the timing for the wars, and so they --that's why they were in the military, and they needed the combat experience. So, as a result, he didn't go to Vietnam. And we were talking about it again, and I said, You know, I don't think you would have made it through another war, not with his attitude.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: When you enlisted, you enlisted as an enlisted man or were you enlisted as an officer?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And how did you raise your ranks to lieutenant and then to captain?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Seven months after I was within the Army, I was a lieutenant.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And then you stayed lieutenant through World War I?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Any promotions during World War -

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: World War II. I'm sorry. You're right. World War II. Any promotions during that time?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. And then raised to rank of captain during the Korean conflicts?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And retired as captain or retired as what rank?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Full colonel. And your promotions were based on career moves and training and education, right?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I would tell you that he was promoted above --what is the term, I have forgotten what it is now --out of zone twice, sooner than he should have been because of his experience and so forth. Again, I had the West Pointers, and that's kind of unusual because the West Pointers are, well, I mean, you know, West Pointers.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: But --but he was always twice out of zone, so he was ahead of his contemporaries, who were West Pointers. I guess that's what I'm trying to say.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Today as a veteran of two major wars, but certainly observed many others, what is your feeling about war today?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, I think --I think it is terrible. I just --I just don't think it is -people need to be fighting.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: No, but if you have got to do it, then I don't mind doing it.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: It is just part of my life, I guess.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Uh-huh. After Korea, what did you do?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Career wise, what did you do after?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: That's when you went to flight school and jump school.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, jump school and then flight.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: --twice. He was --oh, I think the Fulda Gap was kind of interesting, Ron.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: We were stationed on the Russian border.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: In Fulda. You ever heard of Fulda?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: In Russia and West Germany or East Germany, there is a gap, just --you can see it on the map. And you get a map that is --got all the humps and everything on it, you can see this gap that comes right straight in, and we were up there after the war at Fulda.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Tell them about --tell them about the --the fact that our people couldn't be -couldn't be armed, our aircraft couldn't be armed.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We patrol the border. Our aircraft couldn't be --our helicopters couldn't be armed.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: --and Russians, they were armed. And --and they had a couple of --I was a pilot for the Army Aviator, and we had guys that just had to land real fast and keep away from the -MRS. PITTENGER: They were forced.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: They were trying to circle and bring them in and put them down in the east zone.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: And these guys had to evade and come back and land on our side. And there was a major incident. We had a guy from Time Magazine come over and --and I guess he stayed with us now that I think about it --and did the interview on it. And as a result of the incident at the Fulda Gap of one of our guys being on --taken down on their side, they changed the rulings, and you were allowed to arm your aircraft after that.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: I mean, how ridiculous can you get.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: So I understand after Korea, then you moved into Army Air Corps.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. One would say fighter pilot.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: Really because of his command. It was just another skill. It didn't really --it was just another skill.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: But more for his command ability was what I was saying.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And as a pilot now, you were flying where in the country?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. In Korea or in Germany?

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: In the States. Okay. And then you retired?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: When we went back to Germany one of the times, Ron had broken the cartilage in his leg, and they wouldn't operate because he was in school, and he couldn't finish his school, so he just hobbled back and forth, which added to the stress at that point, I'm going to add, too. We --you were --did --let me think a minute. Lost my train of thought. Sorry. Oh, I know, if the Lunar Module had gone down in Africa -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Well, that's all I knew was that if it went down, we were on alert to go -

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: As it was, it was able to return where they wanted it to, but if it had done the splashdown thing, the helicopters would have had to retrieve it, so that was -

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Never happened so I don't consider it to be very important.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: Okay. Is there anything else you want to add that we haven't covered dealing with your years of service?

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Not that I can think of.

sp.speaker: Ronald R. Pittenger
sp.p: Maybe my wife could think of something I've told her.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Pittenger
sp.p: You know, there is so much. Try to condense 87 years into two hours is --you know, and he wouldn't brag, but I would tell you that he was my hero.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: No question about that. Well, I thank you for interview. Of course, we thank you for your service to the country, no question about that.

sp.speaker: David Emory
sp.p: And no question. And off the record now. [Conclusion of interview]
